findings.claim: "In 1920 a Model T Ford cost a worker about three months' wages. By 1925 the same car cost three weeks' wages."
findings.truth: A Model T at under $300 (the lesson's own 1925 price) was about three months' wages for a worker on $25-30 a week. Ford's own $5 a day is about $30 a week, so three weeks' wages was roughly $90. Rewritten around the price the lesson already gives.
findings.evidence: internal: the same lesson gives the 1925 price as under $300 and Ford's wage as $5 a day

findings.claim: The Fordney-McCumber Tariff "raised import duties on foreign goods by an average of 38%" (repeated in a flashcard, a match card and two mark schemes).
findings.truth: The Act set the average ad valorem rate on dutiable imports AT about 38.5%; it did not raise duties BY 38%.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Fordney-McCumber Tariff': 'raised the American ad valorem tariff rate to an average of about 38.5% for dutiable imports'

findings.claim: "Examiner reports flag students who write a chronology of events."
findings.truth: Invented exam claim. The advice stands without it.
findings.evidence: checker brief: invented examiner claims are removed

findings.claim: "Petrol stations multiplied from a few hundred in 1920 to over 120,000 by 1929."
findings.truth: The 1929 figure is standard but the 1920 one looks far too low - the USA already had thousands of drive-in filling stations by 1920. No source found within this session's fetch budget, so left as written.

findings.claim: "While one third of Americans bought their first refrigerator, another third lived in homes without electricity."
findings.truth: Refrigerators were still a luxury: Lesson 1 gives annual sales of about 800,000 by 1929 against roughly 30 million households, so nowhere near a third. Radio is the accurate 'one third' - 10 million households owned a set.
findings.evidence: internal: Lesson 1 (refrigerator sales, 10 million radio households) and Lesson 3

findings.claim: "Only about 1.5 million of the country's 30 million households" bought shares, against the key fact's "around three million Americans owned shares".
findings.truth: Two different share-ownership figures in one lesson. Made consistent with the key fact.

findings.claim: "Vague phrases like 'some people did not benefit' cap students at the lower bands."
findings.truth: Invented mark-scheme claim.

findings.claim: "The average factory shift fell from 60 hours in 1900 to under 50 by 1929."
findings.truth: 60 hours was the working week, not a shift.
findings.evidence: self-evident; standard figures are for the week

findings.claim: Talkies brought "new performers like Greta Garbo and James Cagney".
findings.truth: Garbo was already an MGM silent star from 1925-26; she is the classic example of a silent star who survived the transition. Cagney is a genuine talkie arrival.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Greta Garbo' (MGM contract 1925; first sound film 1930)

findings.claim: "Examiners reward links across the unit, not isolated description."
findings.truth: Invented exam claim.

findings.claim: Card 7 answer "1926." and card 10 answer "The Charleston."
findings.truth: Bare one-word answers; both given a fuller answer of a few words.
findings.evidence: flashcard rules in the checker brief

findings.claim: "By 1929 there were over 23,000 cinemas in the USA - more than there were post offices."
findings.truth: The USA had roughly twice as many post offices as cinemas in this period (about 45,000-49,000 offices), so the comparison is almost certainly wrong. No postal count could be sourced this session, so left as written.

findings.claim: "The 1922 Hays Office ... introduced a code that censored on-screen drinking, nudity and crime."
findings.truth: The office was set up in 1922, but its 'Don'ts and Be Carefuls' list came in 1927 and the Production Code in 1930. A common textbook compression rather than a mark-affecting error.

findings.claim: The 1927 Snyder-Gray trial "complete with a smuggled photograph of Snyder's electrocution".
findings.truth: The trial was in 1927; the smuggled execution photograph ran on the Daily News front page in January 1928.

findings.claim: Conclusion: "Cinema (110 million tickets a week by 1929)".
findings.truth: The lesson body, its flashcards and two mark schemes all say about 100 million a week. Conclusion brought into line.

findings.claim: Radio: "Within a decade nearly half of all American households owned a set."
findings.truth: 10 million sets against about 30 million households is roughly a third. Lesson 9 says radio reached 28 million households only by 1939.

findings.claim: "The boxer Jack Dempsey's 1926 fight with Gene Tunney drew the first $2 million gate" (repeated in a mark scheme).
findings.truth: The 1926 Philadelphia fight took about $1.9 million. Boxing's first two-million-dollar gate was the September 1927 Chicago rematch.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Jack Dempsey': the 1927 rematch 'brought in a record-setting $2 million gate ... the sport's first two-million-dollar gate'

findings.claim: "The suffrage movement led by figures like Carrie Chapman Catt had campaigned since the 1880s."
findings.truth: The movement dates from the 1840s (Seneca Falls, 1848) - as the lesson's own glossary entry says.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the glossary entry in the same lesson

findings.claim: Wilson "told Congress in 1918 that votes for women were 'vital to the winning of the war'".
findings.truth: A paraphrase presented as a quotation. Wilson addressed the Senate on 30 September 1918 and called suffrage 'vitally essential to the successful prosecution of the great war of humanity'. He also backed state-level suffrage in 1916 rather than opposing suffrage outright. Quotation marks removed.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution' (Wilson's 30 September 1918 Senate address)

findings.claim: The 19th Amendment "gave women the right to vote in federal elections" (repeated in the correct option of a knowledge check, a flashcard and a mark scheme).
findings.truth: The amendment forbids denying the vote on account of sex in any election, state or federal. The lesson elsewhere says correctly that women could vote in every state.
findings.evidence: text of the 19th Amendment; internal contradiction with the same lesson

findings.claim: "Electricity reached ... about 25% of farms" by 1929 (repeated in a flashcard and a mark scheme).
findings.truth: Only about 3% of farm homes had electricity in the early 1930s, before the Rural Electrification Administration. Changed to 'fewer than one farm in ten'.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Rural Electrification Act': 'ninety percent of farm homes ... electrified [by 1959], compared to three percent in the early 1930s'

findings.claim: "Examiner reports flag students who treat the flapper image as proof that all women were liberated."
findings.truth: Invented exam claim.

findings.claim: Card 3 answer "Clara Bow."
findings.truth: Bare answer given a fuller answer.
findings.evidence: flashcard rules in the checker brief

findings.claim: "Around 25,000 American women had served as nurses near the front."
findings.truth: About 25,000 American women served overseas in all roles - nurses, telephone operators, Red Cross and canteen workers. The nurses were a large part, not the whole.

findings.claim: "For an 8-mark Explain Significance question on Sacco and Vanzetti..." and advice to weigh four factors in the 12-mark essay.
findings.truth: This paper's period study sets six compulsory questions: how interpretations differ (4), why they differ (4), how convincing (8), describe two features (4), 'in what ways' (8) and an essay built on two identified aspects (12). It sets no significance question - that belongs to the thematic study on the other paper - and the essay is built on two bullets, not four factors.
findings.evidence: spec section 4.4.1, question table and notes for questions 1-6

findings.claim: Practice question 6: "Explain the significance of the Sacco and Vanzetti case for divisions in 1920s America", labelled 8 marks.
findings.truth: Same problem: reworded to the 'In what ways...' form this paper actually uses, which the existing mark scheme already fits.

findings.claim: "Convicted in 1921 and, after seven years of appeals, executed in August 1927" (repeated in a flashcard and a mark scheme).
findings.truth: July 1921 to August 1927 is six years.
findings.evidence: arithmetic on the lesson's own dates

findings.claim: Key fact: "Examiners reward students who explain its significance in those terms, not just retell the story."
findings.truth: Invented exam claim inside content_html.

findings.claim: Collapsible: "Treat these as one connected backlash ... that is how examiners reward an answer."
findings.truth: Invented exam claim inside content_html.

findings.claim: Judge Webster Thayer "openly described the men as 'anarchist bastards'".
findings.truth: The reported wording is 'anarchistic bastards' (Thayer to Professor Richardson). Left as written because the reported wording itself varies between accounts.

findings.claim: The Bonus Army "camped on the Anacostia Flats just across the Potomac from the Capitol".
findings.truth: The Anacostia Flats lie across the Anacostia River.

findings.claim: "A common misconception examiners flag is that the Crash itself caused the Depression directly."
findings.truth: Invented exam claim; the point itself is sound and kept.

findings.claim: Black Sunday was "one of around fourteen major storms that year" (1935; repeated in the glossary, a flashcard and a mark scheme).
findings.truth: Fourteen is the figure usually given for 1932; 1935 saw far more (about forty). Two fetches failed to produce a sourced annual table, so the claim is left as written rather than swapped for an unsourced number.

findings.claim: "A consortium of bankers led by Richard Whitney intervened."
findings.truth: Whitney placed the bids as the pool's agent; the pool was led by Thomas Lamont of J.P. Morgan.

findings.claim: Mark scheme: "Hoover refused to invite reporters into the White House."
findings.truth: Hoover held regular White House press conferences, especially early in his term; relations soured later. Could not be sourced this session, so left as written.

findings.claim: Hoover "insisted ... that 'prosperity is just around the corner'".
findings.truth: The phrase is universally attached to Hoover in textbooks but is not documented as his words. Left as written because GCSE material treats it as his.

findings.claim: Fireside chats reached "60 million homes that owned a radio" (repeated in a flashcard and two mark schemes).
findings.truth: There were only about 30 million American households in 1933, and Lesson 9 says radio reached 28 million households by 1939. 60 million is impossible as a household figure.
findings.evidence: internal: Lesson 9 gives 28 million radio households in 1939

findings.claim: The PWA "funded large infrastructure projects - the Hoover Dam, the Lincoln Tunnel, the Triborough Bridge" (repeated in a flashcard and a mark scheme).
findings.truth: The Hoover Dam was begun in 1931 under the Boulder Canyon Project, as Lesson 7 says. Grand Coulee is the flagship PWA dam; the Lincoln Tunnel and Triborough Bridge are correct.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with Lesson 7; Wikipedia 'Public Works Administration'

findings.claim: "Examiner reports flag students who write 'agency soup'."
findings.truth: Invented exam claim; the advice is kept.

findings.claim: "In June 1933 the Glass-Steagall Act ... created the FDIC which insured personal deposits up to $5,000."
findings.truth: The 1933 Act's insurance limit was $2,500 from January 1934; $5,000 came with the Banking Act of 1935. Reworded so the $5,000 in the flashcards stays correct.

findings.claim: Federal Project Number One "producing post office murals, the Federal Theatre Project and Dorothea Lange's photographs of migrant workers".
findings.truth: Lange photographed for the Resettlement Administration and its successor the Farm Security Administration, not the WPA arts project; most post-office murals came from the Treasury Section of Fine Arts.

findings.claim: "Examiner reports flag the misconception that the New Deal ended the Depression."
findings.truth: Invented exam claim.

findings.claim: Key fact: the New Deal "largely failed African-Americans, Mexican-Americans and Native Americans".
findings.truth: The lesson body credits Native Americans with real gains under the 1934 Indian Reorganization Act, and the conclusion lists domestic workers instead. Key fact aligned with the conclusion.

findings.claim: Card 3 answer "Federal pensions, unemployment insurance and aid to dependent children."
findings.truth: A comma list fails the validator; replaced with a single idea (federal old-age pensions funded by payroll taxes).
findings.evidence: flashcard rules in the checker brief

findings.claim: The Tuskegee Airmen "flew over 15,000 missions" (glossary, flashcard and knowledge check repeat it), and the glossary adds that they flew "without losing a single bomber they were escorting on most days".
findings.truth: They flew 1,578 missions - 15,533 combat SORTIES. The 'never lost a bomber' claim is a documented myth: 27 escorted bombers were shot down, still far better than the 46-per-group average.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Tuskegee Airmen': 1,578 combat missions; Air Force Historical Research Agency found 27 bombers lost

findings.claim: Cards 1, 3 and 14 answered "March 1941.", "7 December 1941." and "Harry Truman."
findings.truth: Bare answers; each given a fuller answer of a few words.
findings.evidence: flashcard rules in the checker brief

findings.claim: "Henry Kaiser's shipyards launched a Liberty cargo ship in just 4-5 days."
findings.truth: Four days and fifteen hours was a one-off publicity record (the Robert E. Peary); the routine Kaiser build time was a fortnight or more. Widely repeated in textbooks, so left as written.

findings.claim: "Federal spending rose from $9 billion in 1939 to $98 billion by 1944."
findings.truth: Federal outlays were about $91 billion in FY1944 and $92.7 billion in FY1945. $98 billion is the common textbook rounding of wartime peak spending; left as written.
findings.evidence: no authoritative source fetched this session

findings.claim: "A Levittown three-bedroom house went up in around 16 minutes of labour."
findings.truth: 16 minutes was the interval between completed houses at peak (about 30 a day), not the labour a house took.

findings.claim: "Contrasting interpretations of post-war America are common. Examiners reward students who can show..."
findings.truth: Two invented exam claims (frequency and reward) in one sentence.

findings.claim: Card 12: "Name three rock and roll artists..." / "Elvis Presley, Chuck Berry and Little Richard."
findings.truth: A list answer fails the validator; rewritten as a single-idea card on Elvis Presley.
findings.evidence: flashcard rules in the checker brief

findings.claim: "Female employment rose to around 19 million by 1960" (repeated in a mark scheme).
findings.truth: 19 million is the 1944 wartime figure this unit uses in Lesson 10; the 1960 female labour force was over 20 million. No sourced 1960 figure was obtained this session, so left as written.

findings.claim: "In June 1950 Julius Rosenberg ... was arrested. His wife Ethel was arrested two months later" (repeated in two mark schemes).
findings.truth: Julius was arrested on 17 July 1950 and Ethel on 11 August 1950 - three weeks apart. June 1950 is the arrest of David Greenglass.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Julius and Ethel Rosenberg': Julius arrested 17 July 1950, Ethel 11 August 1950

findings.claim: "The case was prosecuted by a young Republican congressman named Richard Nixon" (a flashcard asks who 'prosecuted Hiss').
findings.truth: Nixon drove the case as a member of HUAC; a US attorney prosecuted the perjury trials. A congressman cannot prosecute.

findings.claim: "Through 1950 to 1954 McCarthy used his Senate Committee on Government Operations to investigate..."
findings.truth: McCarthy only chaired that committee from January 1953 - as the lesson's own mark scheme says ('chairmanship ... 1953-54').
findings.evidence: internal contradiction within Lesson 12; Wikipedia 'Joseph McCarthy'

findings.claim: "Eisenhower privately disliked him but said publicly he 'would not get in the gutter with that guy'."
findings.truth: The remark was made privately to his staff, so the sentence contradicts itself.

findings.claim: "Contrasting interpretations are common" on McCarthyism.
findings.truth: Claim about what the exam commonly sets; reworded to describe the historiography instead.

findings.claim: Card 2: "Name three Cold War events..." / "Soviet atomic bomb (1949), Communist victory in China (1949), Korean War (1950)."
findings.truth: A list answer fails the validator; rewritten as a single-idea card on the Soviet bomb.
findings.evidence: flashcard rules in the checker brief

findings.claim: "The Senate voted 67-22 to formally censure McCarthy for 'conduct unbecoming'."
findings.truth: The vote and date are right, but the resolution 'condemned' him and did not use the phrase 'conduct unbecoming'.

findings.claim: Collapsible opens: "Examiner reports flag a recurring student weakness..."
findings.truth: Invented exam claim inside content_html; the point is kept without it.

findings.claim: "Examiner reports stress that ordinary participants ... mattered as much as the leaders."
findings.truth: Invented exam claim.

findings.claim: "In southern states, fewer than 5% of eligible black voters were registered" in 1954 (repeated in the key fact).
findings.truth: That figure fits Mississippi, not the South as a whole - roughly a fifth of voting-age black southerners were registered by the early 1950s, and the lesson itself gives Mississippi at about 7% in 1964. No sourced figure could be fetched this session, so it is flagged rather than changed. Recommended fix: name Mississippi rather than 'southern states'.

findings.claim: Mark scheme: Johnson pushed the 1964 Act through "despite an 83-day southern filibuster".
findings.truth: The Senate filibuster on the Civil Rights Act is normally given as 54-60 days; 83 days is the whole floor debate at most. Could not be settled this session.

findings.claim: "By 1968 around half a million American troops were in Vietnam and around 16,500 had been killed."
findings.truth: 16,899 Americans died in 1968 alone; the cumulative toll by the end of 1968 was about 36,900 of the war's 58,220.
findings.evidence: National Archives, Vietnam War U.S. Military Fatal Casualty Statistics (1965: 1,928; 1966: 6,350; 1967: 11,363; 1968: 16,899)

findings.claim: "Examiner reports flag students who treat Vietnam as separate from the reform programme."
findings.truth: Invented exam claim.

findings.claim: "The Supreme Court's 1972 ruling in Reed v Reed extended equal-protection guarantees to women" (dated 1972 in the conclusion, a mark scheme and the exam tip too).
findings.truth: Reed v Reed was decided on 22 November 1971. The spec, however, names 'the Supreme Court ruling on equal rights (1972)', so the lesson's date matches the spec while the case does not. Options: (a) correct to 1971 and keep the spec link with a clause such as 'decided in November 1971 and usually listed with the 1972 equal-rights ruling'; (b) leave 1972 to match the spec wording exactly. Recommend (a) - four fields to touch, no ripple beyond the date.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Reed v. Reed' (decided 22 November 1971); spec Part three bullet 3
findings.ruling: Option (a): decided November 1971; spec's 1972 listing kept in a clause.

findings.claim: Card 1 answer "The New Frontier."
findings.truth: Bare answer given a fuller answer.
findings.evidence: flashcard rules in the checker brief

findings.claim: One mark scheme says NOW was founded by "Friedan, Pauli Murray, Aileen Hernandez and 24 others" (27); the lesson and a flashcard say 28.
findings.truth: NOW was founded by 28 women. A one-person discrepancy inside a mark scheme.

summary: Fourteen lessons checked against the spec's assessment section: the period study is six compulsory questions worth 4/4/8/4/8/12 and the practice sets and tariffs match it, so the exam framing is sound apart from one HIGH breach - an 'Explain Significance' question type that this paper does not set (it belongs to the thematic study on the other paper). 79 edits also strip fourteen invented examiner claims (three of them inside content_html) and correct a run of wrong figures, dates and attributions: the Model T 'three weeks' wages', Fordney-McCumber raising duties 'by 38%', boxing's first $2 million gate dated to 1926, the 19th Amendment as a federal-elections-only measure, farm electrification at 25%, six years of Sacco and Vanzetti appeals called seven, the Bonus Army camped 'across the Potomac', fireside chats reaching '60 million homes', the PWA building the Hoover Dam, Dorothea Lange working for the WPA, 15,000 Tuskegee 'missions' plus the never-lost-a-bomber myth, Levittown built in '16 minutes of labour', the Rosenberg arrest in 'June 1950', Nixon 'prosecuting' Hiss, McCarthy's committee back-dated to 1950 and 16,500 US dead in Vietnam by 1968. One ADJUDICATE (Reed v Reed dated 1972 against a November 1971 decision, where the spec itself says 1972) and seventeen notes. Lesson 7 needed no edits.
